chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-01.title: Play out nine more games
chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-01.body:
The match is decided within $9$ more games ($Y$ needs $4$ more, $F$ needs $6$ more, and $3+5+1=9$). Imagine that nine games are always played. Fiona wins the match iff she wins at least $6$ of the $9$, i.e. Yor wins at most $3$ of them. With $P(\text{Yor wins a game})=\frac23$:
$$P=\frac1{3^9}\left[\binom90+2\binom91+2^2\binom92+2^3\binom93\right]=\frac{1+18+144+672}{3^9}=\frac{835}{19683}.$$
$835=5\cdot167$ is coprime to $3$, so $m=835$.

**Answer: 835**

chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-01.title: Recursion
chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-01.body:
Let $p(y,f)$ be Fiona's winning probability when Yor has $y$ and Fiona $f$ games: $p(y,6)=1$, $p(6,f)=0$ and $p(y,f)=\frac23p(y+1,f)+\frac13p(y,f+1)$. Computing down from $p(2,0)$ with exact fractions gives $\frac{835}{19683}$, so $m=835$.

**Answer: 835**

chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-02.title: Complex numbers
chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-02.body:
Let $J_n,E_n$ be the positions after $n$ rounds, $J_0=0$, $E_0=1$, and $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/3}$. A round is: $J_{n+1}=E_n+\zeta(J_n-E_n)$, then $E_{n+1}=E_n+\frac12(J_{n+1}-E_n)$. So $E_n-J_{n+1}=\zeta\,(E_n-J_n)$ and $E_{n+1}-J_{n+1}=\frac12(E_n-J_{n+1})$, giving
$$E_{n+1}-J_{n+1}=\tfrac\zeta2(E_n-J_n).$$
Triangle $J_n,E_n,J_{n+1}$ is isosceles with apex angle $120^\circ$ at $E_n$, so $J_{n+1}-J_n=\sqrt3e^{-i\pi/6}(E_n-J_n)$, and thus $J_{n+1}-J_n=\left(\frac\zeta2\right)^n(J_1-J_0)$ with $J_1-J_0=\sqrt3e^{-i\pi/6}$ (since $E_0-J_0=1$).

$$P=J_0+\sum_{n\ge0}(J_{n+1}-J_n)=\frac{\sqrt3e^{-i\pi/6}}{1-\zeta/2}=\frac{4\sqrt3\,e^{-i\pi/6}}{5-i\sqrt3}.$$
Hence $|P|=\frac{4\sqrt3}{\sqrt{25+3}}=\frac{4\sqrt3}{2\sqrt7}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{\sqrt7}=\frac{2\sqrt{21}}7$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt{21}}{7}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-02.title: Numerical check
chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-02.body:
Iterating the two moves $200$ times with complex arithmetic gives $|J_n|\to1.30931\ldots=\frac{2\sqrt{21}}7$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt{21}}{7}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-03.title: Reduce to one variable
chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-03.body:
Let $|a|=r^2$, so $|b|=|c|=\frac1r$. Rotating everything, assume $a=r^2>0$ and $b=\frac1re^{i\theta}$, $c=\frac1re^{i\theta_2}$. From $a+b+c=0$ the imaginary parts cancel, so $\theta_2=-\theta$ (note $\theta=\arg\frac ba$), and $r^2+\frac2r\cos\theta=0$, i.e. $r^3=-2\cos\theta$.

Then $-a^6+b^6+c^6=-r^{12}+\frac2{r^6}\cos6\theta=-16\cos^4\theta+\frac{\cos6\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}$. With $\cos6\theta=32\cos^6\theta-48\cos^4\theta+18\cos^2\theta-1$,
$$-a^6+b^6+c^6=\frac{-32\cos^6\theta+32\cos^6\theta-48\cos^4\theta+18\cos^2\theta-1}{2\cos^2\theta}=-24\cos^2\theta+9-\frac1{2\cos^2\theta}.$$
With $x=\cos^2\theta$: $\;|\,\cdot\,|=\left|24x+\frac1{2x}-9\right|$. Now $24x+\frac1{2x}\le9\iff48x^2-18x+1\le0\iff\frac{9-\sqrt{33}}{48}\le x\le\frac{9+\sqrt{33}}{48}$, which is exactly the given condition. So the expression is $9-\left(24x+\frac1{2x}\right)\le9-2\sqrt{12}=9-4\sqrt3$ by AM-GM, with equality at $x=\frac1{\sqrt{48}}$, which lies in the allowed interval. The maximum is $9-4\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $9-4\sqrt3$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-03.title: Numerical check
chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-03.body:
Scanning $\cos^2\theta$ over the allowed interval (with $\cos\theta<0$, $r^3=-2\cos\theta$) and evaluating $|-a^6+b^6+c^6|$ directly gives a maximum of $2.0718=9-4\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $9-4\sqrt3$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-04.title: Linearity and rotation
chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-04.body:
The area of $PXQ$ is proportional to the distance from $X$ to line $PQ$, which is a linear function of the position of $X$ on $BC$ (and stays on one side of $PQ$). Hence the expected area is the area at the midpoint: take $X$ to be the midpoint of $BC$.

Let $D,E$ be the reflections of $B,C$ over $P,Q$. Then $DAB$ and $EAC$ are isosceles right triangles with right angles at $A$, so the rotation by $90^\circ$ about $A$ maps $C\to E$, $D\to B$; hence $CD\perp EB$ and $CD=BE$. By the midline theorem ($P,X,Q$ are midpoints of $BD$, $BC$, $CE$) triangle $PXQ$ is right isosceles with legs $PX=\frac{CD}2$, $XQ=\frac{BE}2$. So $[PXQ]=\frac12\left(\frac{CD}2\right)^2=\frac{CD^2}8$.

In $\triangle CAD$: $AD=AB=4$, $\angle CAD=\angle CAB+90^\circ$, $\cos\angle CAB=\frac{16+36-25}{48}=\frac9{16}$, $\sin\angle CAB=\frac{5\sqrt7}{16}$. So $\cos\angle CAD=-\frac{5\sqrt7}{16}$ and
$$CD^2=6^2+4^2+2\cdot6\cdot4\cdot\frac{5\sqrt7}{16}=52+15\sqrt7.$$
The expected area is $\frac{52+15\sqrt7}8$.

**Answer: $\frac{52+15\sqrt7}{8}$**

chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-04.title: Numerical check
chmmc-cmm-2023-tiebreaker-04.body:
Averaging the area of $PXQ$ over $100000$ equally spaced points of $BC$ gives $11.46078\ldots=\frac{52+15\sqrt7}8$.

**Answer: $\frac{52+15\sqrt7}{8}$**
